key_insight: Large language models used for medical advice encode and express particular ethical priorities rather than a neutral, single ‘‘correct’’ stance; the paper provides a systematic framework to audit and characterize this value pluralism in clinical ethics.
problem_solved: There is no systematic way to examine which bioethical principles (e.g., autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice) guide LLM medical advice and how models differ or conflict; this work fills that gap by operationalizing and measuring ethical pluralism in clinical responses.
method: Define an operational taxonomy of core clinical ethics principles and potential value trade-offs relevant to medical vignettes.
Apply a structured auditing protocol: present standardized clinical scenarios to LLMs, collect responses, and code them against the ethics taxonomy to reveal dominant principles and conflicts.
Quantify pluralism and disagreement using summary metrics (e.g., principle prevalence, inter-model variability, sensitivity to prompt/context) to compare models and settings.
impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners concrete tools to surface, quantify, and compare the ethical orientations of clinical LLMs, enabling safer deployment, more transparent alignment choices, and informed risk mitigation when values conflict.
visual_elements: Flowchart of the auditing framework: inputs (vignettes) → coding rubric (ethics taxonomy) → metrics dashboard (pluralism scores).
Stacked bar or radar chart showing relative emphasis on autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice across models or prompts.
Side-by-side vignette example with two model responses annotated to highlight which ethical principles each prioritizes.
Heatmap of inter-model agreement on principle assignment across a suite of clinical scenarios.
paper_title: What Does the AI Doctor Value? Auditing Pluralism in the Clinical Ethics of Language Models
paper_authors: Payal Chandak, Victoria Alkin, David Wu, Maya Dagan, Taposh Dutta Roy
